valuation.quote_listing: NYSE (primary analysis listing; also TSX: AAUC.TO at C$33.00, consistent at USD/CAD 1.4155)

bull_thesis: Allied Gold is no longer a story about mine ramp-ups — it is a signed, all-cash takeover trading at a very wide discount to its deal price. On January 26, 2026, Zijin Gold International agreed to buy every Allied share for C$44.00 in cash (about US$31.10 at today's exchange rate), a roughly C$5.5 billion deal with no financing condition. Since then nearly every box has been ticked: shareholders approved the deal on March 31 with the required two-thirds majority, Canada completed its approvals under the Investment Canada Act on May 29, and the West African and East African competition authorities (ECOWAS and COMESA) have cleared it. The single remaining condition is China's outbound-investment approval (led by the National Development and Reform Commission, the NDRC — China's economic planning agency that must sign off when a Chinese company buys abroad). The two companies extended the deal's outside date (the deadline after which either side can walk away) to July 29, 2026, and on June 10 — after gold had already fallen sharply — both publicly restated that they are fully committed to closing. Meanwhile the underlying business keeps getting better, which strengthens the buyer's incentive to finish: Allied delivered 379,081 ounces in 2025 against guidance of above 375,000, posted a record 117,004-ounce fourth quarter with all-in sustaining costs (the industry's full cash cost per ounce) improving to about $1,980, completed the first-phase expansion at its Sadiola mine in Mali, and its transformational Kurmuk mine in Ethiopia — roughly 290,000 low-cost ounces a year once ramped — is on budget and within weeks of first gold, with the Ethiopian government publicly backing the transaction. At $23.36 the stock offers roughly a third more if the deal closes at terms within weeks, and even the walk-away scenario leaves you owning a producer heading from about 380,000 toward 800,000 ounces a year with net cash of $178 million on the March balance sheet. Conditions that must hold: Chinese approval arrives by (or shortly after) July 29, and neither party uses the deadline to force a price cut.
bear_thesis: The market is not pricing a 33% discount to a signed cash deal for no reason. Gold has fallen from above $5,500 an ounce around deal signing to about $4,100 today — a decline of roughly a quarter — which means Zijin agreed to a price struck at the top of the gold market. The one approval still outstanding is the one from the buyer's own government, and press reports suggest China's regulator has questioned whether the C$44 price is still defensible at lower gold prices. The July 29 outside date has already been extended once, and any further extension requires mutual agreement — handing Zijin a legitimate lever to demand a price cut, or simply walk. Critically, the publicly disclosed C$220 million termination fee is payable by Allied in specified circumstances (such as taking a superior offer); no reverse fee payable by Zijin for a failure of Chinese approval has been confirmed, so the buyer's option to abandon may be cheap. If the deal breaks, the stock does not glide to a analyst's net-asset-value estimate — it gaps to what a jilted West African gold miner fetches in a falling gold tape: the shares traded around C$34-35 before the deal when gold was $5,500, and gold is now 25% lower. The standalone risks the deal has been masking also return in full: Mali is the largest cash generator and the junta there seized Barrick's neighboring Loulo complex in 2025, the fiscal take is punishing (statutory results show a $95 million tax charge on $51 million of pre-tax income in the March quarter — Allied has reported a bottom-line loss in four straight quarters despite record revenue, with trailing-twelve-month earnings per share of negative $1.05), Kurmuk still has to actually ramp in a frontier jurisdiction with a border-region security history, and trailing free cash flow is only about $32 million because expansion spending consumes nearly all operating cash. What would confirm the bear case: July 29 passes without Chinese approval, either party signals renegotiation, or an announcement of a reduced offer price.
sop_fair_value: US$29.00 per share (about C$41) — base case: the C$44.00 all-cash arrangement completes at or near its terms, carried below the full offer value to reflect completion risk and the branch where terms are trimmed to secure the final Chinese approval.
sop_breakdown: The binding deal overlay dominates the sum-of-the-parts (valuing each piece separately): the arrangement consideration is C$44.00 cash per share, about US$31.10 at USD/CAD 1.4155, for roughly 126 million shares (C$5.5 billion). Behind it, the standalone parts at today's ~$4,100 gold: Sadiola in Mali (first-phase expansion complete, 200,000-230,000 ounces a year rising with further expansion) roughly US$1.6-2.0 billion; Kurmuk in Ethiopia (about 290,000 ounces a year in its first four years at low cost, first gold within weeks, net of streaming obligations) roughly US$1.4-1.8 billion; the Côte d'Ivoire mines Bonikro and Agbaou (about 170,000 combined ounces, shorter lives) roughly US$0.5-0.7 billion; plus net cash of US$178 million on the March 2026 balance sheet. That sums to roughly US$26-31 per share of intrinsic standalone value before the discount the market applies to West African single-region producers — which is why the deal price is defensible for the buyer even at today's gold price, and why the adverse case of US$16.50 reflects a broken-deal market-clearing print rather than intrinsic value.
risk_reward: The favorable case is the fixed cash offer, so the upside is capped but large from today's price and resolves within weeks; the adverse case is a deal break into a weak gold tape, where the stock re-rates down to a jilted-miner discount below standalone worth. The reward side is a hard contractual number; the risk side is a market-sentiment number cushioned by real and improving assets — a rare shape where the downside scenario still leaves you holding a business at a discount to its parts. Levels are stated in the valuation block; the deciding variable is a single regulator's decision, not the assets.
peer_comps_note: The peer file (AEM, KGC, EGO, IAG, CDE, AGI, ELD.TO, OGC.TO) carries no populated live multiples for Allied — it is flagged unmapped on the data side — and with a binding all-cash arrangement in force, deal terms supersede multiple-based anchoring anyway. Sanity check: at the C$44 offer the enterprise value is roughly US$3.7 billion, about three times a reasonable 2027 cash-flow estimate once Kurmuk ramps at today's gold price — below where established mid-tier producers such as Agnico or Kinross trade, so the offer is not an outlier the buyer's regulator should choke on; the discount reflects deal risk, not a rich standalone valuation.
forcing_function: July 29, 2026 — the extended outside date of the Zijin arrangement, the deadline by which the last outstanding condition (China's outbound-investment approval) must be met or the parties must mutually agree to extend again. This is a hard, contractual date three weeks away that forces one of three resolutions: approval and closing at C$44 cash, a renegotiation announcement, or a termination. Secondary events inside the same window: Kurmuk's first gold pour (guided within weeks as of early July, which further de-risks the asset the buyer is paying for) and second-quarter results in mid-August if the deal slips.
moderator_conclusion: This is a live merger arbitrage, not a mining thesis, and the debate reduces to one question: does China approve by July 29? The market says probably not — at $23.36 against a US$31.10 cash offer, the shares embed something like a coin flip weighted toward failure. I think the market is over-reading a routine delay. The verifiable record shows a deal moving forward, not stalling: every non-Chinese approval is complete, six months from signing to now is normal for a Chinese outbound review of this size, and — most tellingly — both companies publicly recommitted to closing on June 10, after gold had already fallen 25% from signing levels; a buyer preparing to walk does not do that. The Ethiopian government is publicly supportive, the operator delivered its 2025 guidance (379,081 ounces against a promise of above 375,000, with a record fourth quarter and improving costs), and Kurmuk's imminent first gold makes the asset more valuable to Zijin than the day it signed. The bear case is real but narrower than the price implies: the reported Chinese concern about price defensibility comes from secondary sources, while the primary-source record is consistent with approval-with-delay. What keeps this from maximum conviction is exactly what the risk framework says should: the remaining risk is a single, opaque, foreign-government binary I cannot handicap with an edge, a further extension needs mutual agreement, and no reverse termination fee protecting Allied has been confirmed — so a walk-away is cheap for the buyer if it wants one. The timing call: enter now, sized for a binary, with resolution forced within weeks. If the deal closes at terms the return is the full spread in under two months; if terms are trimmed the likely landing zone still sits above today's price; the loss case is a break into a soft gold tape, cushioned — not eliminated — by a business worth most of today's price on its own. Judged with no catalyst at all, the standalone value case is middling: the parts are worth more than the price, but Mali concentration, a brutal fiscal take that has produced four straight statutory quarterly losses, and thin trailing free cash flow during the build-out cap it at average.

skeptic_self.kill_fact: No disqualifier found. Deal terms (C$44.00 cash, C$5.5B, outside date July 29, 2026), approval status (only Chinese approval outstanding), and delivery record (379,081 oz vs >375,000 guided; record Q4; Kurmuk near first gold) all verified against primary sources: company press releases via GlobeNewswire (Jan 26, Apr 28, May 29, Jun 10, 2026), SEC-filed 6-Ks, and live FMP quotes (AAUC $23.36 NYSE / AAUC.TO C$33.00 cross-checked at USD/CAD 1.4155; gold $4,108). Corrections applied: (1) the claim that China's regulator specifically questions price defensibility traces to low-authority secondary sources — carried as unconfirmed color, not fact; (2) no reverse termination fee payable by Zijin could be confirmed, so the buyer's walk-away option is potentially costless — bear level widened from $17.00 to $16.50 and conviction held at 4 rather than higher; (3) the board transcript and peer file predate the deal entirely (Nov 2025) — the entire thesis was re-underwritten from live sources rather than the stale operational-ramp framing; (4) the input's TTM EPS of -1.05 was verified as tax/fiscal-take driven (e.g. Q1 2026: $95M tax on $51M pre-tax income), not operational deterioration.
